rv.q: All the parts are good. They just, maddeningly, don't add for a stunning show.
For much of the rest of us, this disconcertingly wholesome new version of the 1958. Oscar-winning movie about raising a French courtesan is very pretty and bland.
It's a number built to pop, but like just about everything else, it lacks fizz.

But it inadvertently brought to mind how thoroughly the musical, about a young woman being groomed for a life as a courtesan in turn-of-the-20th-century Paris, has been scrubbed of anything even remotely naughty or distasteful.
This is some very flat champagne.

The attempt to turn such a property into a girl-power fantasy, in part by casting Disney star Vanessa Hudgens as Gigi — and in part by de-perving it completely — has left it more perverted than ever, and altogether unworthy of its name.
Whatever good work Thomas was doing to save "Gigi" from its previous self is undermined by the central performance, which is all at sea even before you ponder the vocal limitations thereof.
All in all, Gigi is a wonderful treat, and Hudgens may find herself welcomed back to Broadway for years to come.

Where: Theatre, 250 W. 52nd St., When: On sale through Oct. 4. Tuesdays and Thursdays at 7 p.m., Fridays at 8 p.m., Wednesdays and Saturdays at 2 p.m. and 8 p.m., Sundays at 3 p.m. How much: $57-$137, call (877) 250-2929 or visit gigionbroadway.
Indeed, they’re as tedious for us to watch as Gigi claims they are.
Ironically, though, Gaston's courtship of Gigi comes across as creepier here than it did when a thirtysomething Louis Jourdan pursued a dewy Leslie Caron (then Hudgens' age) onscreen.
This Gigi is gorgeous to look at and boasts a fine performance from Vanessa Hudgens in the title role, but it's dramatically inert and musically disappointing.
Yet the new revival of Gigi too often feels akin to dirty linen that’s been put through the wash too many times; it’s clean now and has a sheen, but it’s threadbare, intellectually and emotionally.
When all is said and done, Gigi is an insubstantial property, despite a peerless score by Lerner and Loewe.
The result, however, is a bland soufflé that is too hard on the outside and too soft at the center.
Otherwise, 'Gigi' is the night the Champagne went flat.
If it comes to that, this whole Gigi is lacking in charm, if not nerve.
Hudgens gives the sort of sincere but clumsy performance you’d expect to see in, well, a high school musical.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Musical

cn.t: Critics find this Gigi revival pretty but bland, with a dated story that fails to charm despite attempts at feminist updates. Hudgens receives mixed notices, while Victoria Clark earns praise and the Lerner-Loewe score remains a highlight.

sg.ra: For MJ the Musical's dance-heavy choreography, Center Orchestra rows A-H sit entirely in front of the mezzanine overhang (which begins at row J) and deliver head-on sightlines of the performers' feet — critical for a Michael Jackson dance biomusical. Row A seats 107-110 are frequently cited as the theatre's best, but rows C-D balance proximity with neck-angle comfort.

Because Neil Simon's orchestra is unusually deep (25 rows, A-Z) and the mezzanine overhang only starts cutting the top of the stage noticeably by row S, rows H-P give you full head-on views with no overhang effect at non-premium pricing — a specific quirk of this house's long orchestra footprint.

The mezzanine overhang is felt from row J onward and by rows S-Z it actively cuts off the top of the stage per SeatPlan's orchestra guide — a real issue for MJ the Musical, which uses tall set pieces and lifts. Unique to Neil Simon because the orchestra runs all the way to row Z, pushing rear seats deep under the overhang.

Front Center Mezzanine rows A-B give an elevated, unobstructed sweep — particularly valuable at Neil Simon because MJ the Musical uses formation choreography that reads better from above. Tripadvisor users confirm no obstruction issues at front mezz (photo cited from row A seat 103). Row A also has the best legroom in the mezzanine.

Specific Neil Simon quirk: Left and Right Mezzanine rows H and L sit directly behind railings that border the internal staircase, making legroom 'very tight' — SeatPlan calls out seats H1-7 and L9-15 by number. This is a house-specific hazard, not the generic 'Broadway legroom is tight' complaint.

Rear mezzanine at Neil Simon has a shallow rake — a specific architectural quirk noted by SeatPlan — so rows S-U feel distant and lose detail on the stage front, and the mezzanine's own underside can minor-obstruct the back-row view. For MJ's facial-expression moments in 'Man in the Mirror' numbers this is a real detriment.

Three boxes are staggered off the Left Mezzanine at Neil Simon — a specific architectural feature of this house — and SeatPlan explicitly states the viewing experience 'isn't the best' because the angle is fully side-on. Priced as premium but not worth it for a dance musical where frontal sightlines matter.
